source_text: Haec ratio seruabatur apud prouidentiam dei pro temporibus omnia modulantis, ne quis ex diuerso ad deiciendam propositionem nostram, cur ergo, dicat, non statim deus aliquam uictus constituit castigationem, quin immo et auxit permissionem? nam in primordio quidem herbidum solummodo et arboreum homini pabulum addixerat: ecce dedi uobis omne faenum sementiuum seminans semen quod est super terram, et omne lignum quod habet in semetipso fructum seminis sementiui uobis erit in escam. postea uero ad Noe enumerata subiectione omnium bestiarum terrae et uolatilium caeli et mouentium in terra et piscium maris et omnis serpentis, erunt, inquit, uobis in escam: uelut holera faeni dedi uobis uniuersa, uerum carnem in sanguine animae suae non edetis. nam et hoc ipso, quod eam solam carnem esui eximit, cuius anima non per sanguinem effunditur, omnis reliquae carnis usum concessisse manifestum est. ad haec respondemus non competisse onerari hominem aliqua adhuc abstinentiae lege, qui cum maxime tam leuem interdictionem unius scilicet pomi tolerare non potuit; remissum itaque illum libertate ipsa corroborandum. aeque post diluuium in reformatione generis humani suffecisse unam interim legem a sanguine abstinendi permisso usu ceterorum. iam enim iudicium dominus ostenderat per diluuium, adhuc etiam comminatus fuerat per exquisitionem sanguinis de manu fratris et de manu bestiae omnis. itaque iustitiam iudicii praeministrans materiam libertatis emisit per ueniam supparans disciplinam, permittens omnia, ut demeret quaedam, plus exacturus, si plus commisisset, abstinentiam imperaturus, cum indulgentiam praemisisset, quo magis, ut diximus, primordiale delictum expiaretur maioris abstinentiae operatione in maioris licentiae occasione.
thought_title: Why God did not impose fasting at first
orientation: Tertullian is answering an objection: if fasting is God's original discipline, why did God not command it from the beginning but instead first gave herbs and later all animals as food?
pass_a_gloss: This rationale was preserved in the providence of God, who modulates all things according to the times, lest anyone from the opposite side, to cast down our proposition, should say: Why then did God not immediately establish some chastisement of food, but rather even increased the permission? For in the beginning indeed he had assigned to man only grassy and tree food: Behold I have given you every seed-bearing plant sowing seed which is upon the earth, and every tree which has in itself fruit of seed-bearing seed will be to you for food. But later, to Noah, after the subjection of all beasts of the earth and birds of heaven and things moving on the earth and fish of the sea and every serpent had been enumerated, they will be, he says, to you for food: as vegetables of grass I have given you all things, but flesh in the blood of its life you shall not eat. For also by this very fact, that he exempts from eating that flesh alone whose life is not poured out through blood, it is clear that he granted the use of all remaining flesh. To these things we answer that it was not fitting for man to be burdened by any law of abstinence yet, who at that very time could not endure so light a prohibition, namely of one fruit; therefore he was to be strengthened by freedom itself, having been let loose. Likewise after the flood, in the reformation of the human race, one law for the time being sufficed, of abstaining from blood, the use of the rest having been permitted. For already the Lord had shown judgment through the flood, and still had threatened through the requiring of blood from the hand of a brother and from the hand of every beast. Therefore, administering beforehand the justice of judgment, he sent out the material of freedom, preparing discipline through pardon, permitting all things, so that he might take away certain things, about to exact more, if he had committed more, about to command abstinence, when he had sent indulgence beforehand, so that more, as we have said, the original sin might be expiated by the working of greater abstinence in the occasion of greater license.

pass_b_english: This was the plan God's providence followed, arranging all things according to their times, so that no one could turn it against us and say: Why then did God not immediately impose some chastisement of food, and instead even increased the permission? For in the beginning he assigned man only grassy and tree food: "See, I have given you every seed-bearing plant that sows seed, which is upon the earth, and every tree that has in itself the fruit of seed that sows seed—it will be food for you" (Genesis 1:29). But later, to Noah, after listing the subjection of all the beasts of the earth, the birds of the sky, the creatures that move on the earth, the fish of the sea, and every serpent, he said: "They will be food for you; like the green plants I have given you all things. But you shall not eat flesh in the blood of its life" (Genesis 9:2-4). For by this very fact—that he exempts from eating only that flesh whose life is not poured out through the blood—it is clear that he granted the use of all other flesh.

To this we answer that it was not fitting for man to be burdened with any law of self-control who was at that very time unable to endure so light a prohibition—that of a single fruit. Therefore he was to be strengthened by freedom itself, having been released. Likewise after the flood, in the renewal of the human race, one law for the time being was enough: to abstain from blood, while the use of everything else was permitted. For the Lord had already shown his judgment through the flood, and he had also threatened the requiring of blood from the hand of a brother and from the hand of every beast (Genesis 9:5). So, administering the justice of judgment beforehand, he sent out the material of freedom, preparing discipline through pardon—permitting all things so that he might take some away, intending to demand more if man committed more, intending to command self-control after he had first granted indulgence. In this way, as we have said, the original sin might be expiated by the working of a greater self-control in the occasion of a greater license.

problems.why: cum maxime means 'when he was especially unable', not 'had just shown'.
problems.fix: who was at that very time unable to endure so light a prohibition

problems.source_quote: remissum itaque illum libertate ipsa corroborandum
problems.why: remissum here means 'relaxed/released from restriction', not 'let loose'; corroborandum is purpose: to be strengthened.
problems.fix: therefore he was to be strengthened by freedom itself, having been released

last_rejected.source_quote: … erunt, inquit, uobis in escam: … verum carnem in sanguine animae suae non edetis.
last_rejected.why: The Latin passage quotes verses 3‑4 about food and blood, not verse 2; the cited range includes verse 2 which is not referenced.
last_rejected.fix: Cite Genesis 9:3‑4 (or just Genesis 9:3‑4) instead of 9:2‑4.
last_rejected.ruling: Latin 'uelut holera faeni dedi uobis uniuersa' matches Gen 9:2-3; citing 9:2-4 is standard acceptable range, not misleading.
